```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

ppnet models a growing bipartite network of events and the people
("perps") who take part in them. The model has two parts, which share no
parameters:

* **the time part**, a Hawkes process for when events happen: a baseline
  rate `mu` plus excitation `K exp(-beta t)` from each past event;
* **the mark part**, who takes part in each event: new perps arrive at a
  rate, and each old perp joins with a probability that depends on their
  history (degree, recency, co-offenders, ...).

This vignette simulates data from the model, then fits the time part and the
mark part separately, as you would build up a model for real data.

```{r}
library(ppnet)
```

## Data

Real data go into `make_events()` as a table of edges (event to perp, with
times) and a table of nodes (with a `role` of `"event"` or `"perp"`). Here
we simulate instead. `attachment_spec()` describes who joins each event:
old perps are weighted by their degree, the time since they last took part
and their number of past co-offenders, and the number of new perps is
negative binomial with at least one perp per event.

```{r}
spec <- attachment_spec(coffenders = TRUE, coffender_window = 20,
                        new_perps = "negbin", min_perps = 1)
truth <- list(mu = 2, K = 0.6, beta = 1.5,
              m = 0.5, beta_edges = 0.1, delta = 0.5, theta = 0.3,
              lambda_new = 0.6, lambda_new0 = 0.4, size_new = 2)
set.seed(1)
ev <- sim_hawkesNet(truth, T_end = 150, mark_type = "ba_bip",
                    attachment = spec, return_net = FALSE)$ev
head(event_summary(ev))
```

## The time part

The two parts share no parameters, so each can be fitted on its own with
`part = "time"` or `part = "marks"`; starting values default to values
worked out from the data. The time part alone is the same model as
`stelfi::fit_hawkes()`:

```{r}
fit_time <- fit_hawkesNet(ev, mark_type = "ba_bip", part = "time")
summary(fit_time)
```

Positive parameters are fitted on the log scale, so their standard errors
come from the delta method and `confint()` gives intervals computed on the
log scale:

```{r}
confint(fit_time)
```

A two-scale kernel (`kernel = "exp2"`) adds a fast component. `AIC()` and
`BIC()` compare fits of the same part as for `glm()`:

```{r}
fit_exp2 <- fit_hawkesNet(ev, mark_type = "ba_bip", part = "time", kernel = "exp2")
AIC(fit_time, fit_exp2)
```

## The mark part

The mark part is fitted the same way. Dropping the co-offender term gives a
nested model, tested with `anova()`:

```{r}
fit_marks <- fit_hawkesNet(ev, mark_type = "ba_bip", part = "marks", attachment = spec)
summary(fit_marks)

spec0 <- attachment_spec(new_perps = "negbin", min_perps = 1)
fit_marks0 <- fit_hawkesNet(ev, mark_type = "ba_bip", part = "marks", attachment = spec0)
anova(fit_marks0, fit_marks)
```

Further terms go into `attachment_spec()`: `paths` (3-paths), `recent`
(own events within `episode_gap`), `random_effect` (individual propensities)
and `cycles` (4-cycles, fitted by pseudo-likelihood, for which `vcov()`
gives sandwich standard errors and likelihood comparisons are refused).
Starting values can still be given for any parameter, e.g.
`params_init = list(theta = 0.5)`, and `fixed_params` holds parameters at
those values.

## Checking a fit

`simulate()` draws new histories from a fitted model. A fit of one part
needs the other part's parameters, here from the time fit:

```{r}
sims <- simulate(fit_marks, nsim = 3, seed = 2, params = coef(fit_time))
c(observed = nrow(ev$times), simulated = vapply(sims, function(s) nrow(s$times), 1))
```

`diag_temporal()` gives time-rescaling residuals for the time part:

```{r}
d <- diag_temporal(ev, fit_time$par)
ks.test(d$tau, "pexp")$p.value
```
